summary: Provides the common definitions for the structure and identification of management information for TCP/IP-based internets, working with companion memos for the MIB and the network management protocol. It was replaced by RFC 1155.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a network can be managed, someone has to say what the manageable things are called and what values they may hold. This RFC defines that common scheme, so that the objects in a MIB and the protocol that reads them are built on one agreed set of rules.

subtitle: The common rules for naming managed objects, describing their values, and versioning them across the SNMP family of documents.

tldr.problem: Network management needs a common way to name the things a manager can read and change, and a common way to describe what values those things may hold, or different vendors' equipment could not be managed together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SMI: objects are named by OBJECT IDENTIFIERs in a global tree, their values come from a small set of permitted ASN.1 types, and each object carries a definition, an access level and a status.
tldr.outcome: The SMI became the shared vocabulary for the MIB and SNMP documents that followed it. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 1155.

facts.label: Permitted primitive types
facts.value: INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, NULL

today: RFC 1065 is an Internet Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1155, so read that document for the current rules.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This memo provides the common definitions for the structure and identification of management information for TCP/IP-based internets. Together with its companion memos, which describe the initial management information base and the initial network management protocol, it provides a simple, workable architecture for managing TCP/IP-based internets and in particular the Internet.

The memo describes the common structures and identification scheme for defining management information, including an object information model for network management and a set of generic types, with formal descriptions given in ASN.1. It is largely concerned with organizational concerns and administrative policy: it neither specifies the objects which are managed nor the protocols used to manage them, which are left to the companion memos.

The memo sets out to achieve two goals, simplicity and extensibility. By fostering a simple SMI, the minimal number of constraints is imposed on future potential approaches, and by fostering an extensible SMI, the maximal number of potential approaches remains available for experimentation. The authors explain that previous experience with network management, while giving the community insight, is hardly conclusive.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a network can be managed, someone has to say what the manageable things are called and what values they may hold. This RFC defines that common scheme, so that the objects in a MIB and the protocol that reads them are built on one agreed set of rules.

sections.title: Names and the OBJECT IDENTIFIER Tree
sections.content:
Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base. Objects in the MIB are defined using ASN.1. Each type of object has a name, a syntax and an encoding, and the name is represented uniquely as an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name.

An OBJECT IDENTIFIER is a sequence of integers that traverse a global tree. The tree consists of a root connected to labeled nodes by edges, and each node may have labeled children of its own, forming a subtree that may continue to an arbitrary depth. Central to the notion is that administrative control of the meanings assigned to the nodes may be delegated as one traverses the tree; a label is a pairing of a brief textual description and an integer. The root node is unlabeled but has at least three children: iso(1), administered by the International Standards Organization, ccitt(2), administered by the International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee, and joint-iso-ccitt(3), jointly administered by the two.

Under iso(1) the ISO has designated one subtree for other national organizations, org(3), and two of its children have been assigned to the US National Bureau of Standards, one of which has been transferred to the US Department of Defense as dod(6). The Internet subtree therefore starts with the prefix 1.3.6.1, and this memo, as an RFC approved by the IAB, specifies the policy under which that subtree is administered. Four nodes are present: directory(1), reserved for a future memo on the use of the OSI Directory; mgmt(2), used to identify objects defined in IAB-approved documents, whose administration is delegated to the Assigned Numbers authority; experimental(3), used for objects used in Internet experiments; and private(4), used for objects defined unilaterally.

Under private(4) there is at least one child, enterprises(1), used among other things to let parties providing networking subsystems register models of their products. An enterprise that receives a subtree may define new MIB objects in it and register its networking subsystems beneath it, so that a fictional Flintstones, Inc. might receive 1.3.6.1.4.1.42 and register its Fred Router at 1.3.6.1.4.1.42.1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: Managed objects are numbered in a tree, like a filing system. The first few numbers are fixed by international standards bodies, and the Internet's part of the tree starts at 1.3.6.1. Below that, a branch is set aside for objects that IAB documents define, one for experiments, and one for companies to use for their own products.

sections.title: Syntax: the Permitted Types
sections.content:
Syntax defines the structure corresponding to an object type, using ASN.1 constructs, although the full generality of ASN.1 is not permitted. Only the primitive types INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER and NULL are allowed, sometimes called non-aggregate types. If an enumerated INTEGER is listed as an object type, a named number with the value 0 shall not be present, because the use of that value is prohibited.

The ASN.1 constructor type SEQUENCE is permitted, provided it is used to generate either lists or tables. A list takes the form SEQUENCE of one or more primitive types, and these types are always present, with no DEFAULT or OPTIONAL clauses. A table takes the form SEQUENCE OF an entry, where the entry resolves to a list constructor.

Application-wide types may also be defined, so long as they resolve into an implicitly defined ASN.1 primitive type, list, table or other application-wide type. Six are defined here. NetworkAddress is a choice representing an address from one of possibly several protocol families, with only the Internet family present at present. IpAddress represents a 32-bit Internet address as an OCTET STRING of length 4 in network byte order, and when encoded with the basic encoding rules only the primitive encoding form shall be used. Counter is a non-negative integer that increases monotonically until it reaches a maximum, when it wraps around and starts again from zero, with a maximum value of 2^32-1. Gauge is a non-negative integer that may increase or decrease but latches at a maximum value, also 2^32-1. TimeTicks counts time in hundredths of a second since some epoch, and the object definition identifies the reference epoch. Opaque passes arbitrary ASN.1 syntax by encoding it with the basic rules into a string of octets which is then encoded as an OCTET STRING, effectively double-wrapping the original value; a conforming implementation need only accept and recognize such data, not unwrap and interpret it.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo allows only four basic value types and lets a list or a table be built from them. On top of those it defines a few ready-made types, such as a counter that only goes up and wraps around, a gauge that can go down but latches at a ceiling, and a tick count measured in hundredths of a second.

sections.title: Managed Objects: Definitions, Access and Status
sections.content:
Although it is not the purpose of the memo to define objects in the MIB, it specifies a format for other memos that do. An object type definition consists of five fields: the OBJECT, a textual name termed the object descriptor together with its object identifier; the Syntax, the abstract syntax for the object type, which must resolve to an instance of the ASN.1 type ObjectSyntax; the Definition, a textual description of the semantics of the object type, which implementations should fulfil because the MIB is intended for use in multi-vendor environments and objects need a consistent meaning across all machines; the Access, one of read-only, read-write, write-only or not-accessible; and the Status, one of mandatory, optional or obsolete.

An object type is a definition of a kind of managed object and is declarative, while an object instance is an instantiation of an object type bound to a value. The notion of an entry in a routing table might be defined in the MIB, and individual entries in a particular routing table which exist at some time are object instances of that object type. The means whereby object instances are referenced is not defined in the MIB; reference is achieved by a protocol-specific mechanism, and it is the responsibility of each management protocol adhering to the SMI to define it.

An object type may be defined so that an instance of it represents an aggregation of information also represented by instances of subordinate object types. A set of such object types is a list, and a table is formed by an aggregation of a list type, so that each instance of the table comprises the set of entries that constitute one table. To afford support for a variety of management protocols, all information by which instances of a given object type may be usefully distinguished is represented by instances of object types defined in the MIB. The OBJECT-TYPE macro is provided to let the key aspects of an object type be represented in a formal way, so that tools can process MIB definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each managed thing is described by five fields: its name, the kind of value it holds, a description of what that value means, whether a manager may read or change it, and whether it must be implemented. A group of such descriptions forms a table, with one entry for each row of real data.

sections.title: Extensions to the MIB
sections.content:
Every Internet-standard MIB document obsoletes all previous such documents. The portion of a name, termed the tail, following the object identifier used to name objects, remains unchanged between versions. New versions may declare old object types obsolete but not delete their names, augment the definition of an object type corresponding to a list by appending non-aggregate object types to the types in the list, or define entirely new object types. New versions may not change the semantics of any previously defined object without changing the name of that object.

These rules admit easier support for multiple versions of the Internet-standard MIB: the semantics associated with the tail of a name remain constant throughout the different versions, so multiple versions may coincide in tail-space and implementations supporting several versions are greatly simplified. As a consequence, a management agent might return an instance corresponding to a superset of the expected object type. Following the principle of robustness, in that case a manager should ignore any additional information beyond the definition of the expected object type, though care is needed with control actions: if an instance does not have the same syntax as its expected object type, then those control actions must fail. In both the monitoring and the control case, the name of an object returned by an operation must be identical to the name requested.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new version of the standard MIB comes out, it can add objects and mark old ones as obsolete, but it must not change what an existing name means. That way, an old manager reading a new MIB sees the extra fields, ignores them, and carries on working.

items.title: OBJECT
items.text: A textual name, the object descriptor, and its corresponding object identifier.

items.title: Syntax
items.text: The abstract syntax for the object type, which must resolve to an instance of the ASN.1 type ObjectSyntax.

items.title: Definition
items.text: A textual description of the semantics of the object type.

items.title: Access
items.text: One of read-only, read-write, write-only, or not-accessible.

items.title: Status
items.text: One of mandatory, optional, or obsolete.
